scenes.say: Launch day. Your one server handles a thousand requests a second. Then a hundred thousand arrive, and it falls over. By the end, you'll scale it, defend your database, and survive a network split.

lines.text: Scale it. Defend it. Survive splits.

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Scale one server to a hundred thousand requests a second. Choose a database and defend it. And answer what happens when the network splits.

scenes.title: One server, 100,000 req/s
scenes.statement: One app server maxes out at 1,000 requests a second. Traffic is 100,000. Scale it without logging users out.
scenes.say: Your app is a hundred times too small. One server tops out at a thousand requests a second. The launch sends a hundred thousand. Fix it, and don't log anyone out while you do.

scenes.head: One server vs the traffic
scenes.say: These bars show requests per second. One server tops out near a thousand. Your traffic is a hundred thousand.

scenes.head: A shop with a long line
scenes.say: A shop has a long line. You can hire a faster cashier, or open more checkouts. A faster cashier hits a limit. More checkouts keep growing, but share one warehouse. In your system, the warehouse is the database.

scenes.head: Vertical vs horizontal
scenes.say: Vertical is one bigger machine. Horizontal is more machines. The good news? Vertical needs no code changes. Horizontal survives losing a box. The catch? No server is a hundred times faster. Horizontal adds moving parts. It needs a front door that spreads requests. And it needs stateless apps: servers that keep no user data between requests.

scenes.head: Load balancer, identical copies
scenes.say: The load balancer is that front door. It spreads requests across identical copies of the app. Add a third copy, and capacity grows by a thousand requests a second. One copy dies, and traffic goes to the others.

scenes.head: Why stateless matters
scenes.say: Now break that rule on purpose. Each server keeps sessions in its own memory. A session is the server's note that you logged in. Ana logs in on server A. The balancer sends her next request to server B. B has never heard of her. She's logged out.
Your turn. Ana must stay logged in, whichever server she lands on. Where do the sessions go? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Where should sessions live so any server works?

scenes.head: State lives outside the app
scenes.say: A shared store. The usual pick is Redis, a fast in-memory store every server can reach. Memory or disk on one machine only helps that machine. A bigger server is still one machine. Now any server can read Ana's session. Redis also holds the cache: copies of popular data, kept in memory. Durable data stays in the database. Kill a server and nobody is logged out. That's how a hundred copies reach a hundred thousand.

scenes.title: One database, many servers
scenes.statement: Every app server hits one database. Reads and writes pile up on one machine.
scenes.say: Copying the app was the easy part. Every copy still talks to one database. Ten thousand queries a second hit that one machine. It has to keep up. And people must still see their own posts.

scenes.head: Replicas, and replica lag
scenes.say: App servers are easy to copy. The database is not. Writes go to one primary, which copies them to read replicas. A user posts a comment and refreshes. The replica hasn't caught up, so the comment is gone. That's replica lag. For your own fresh writes, read from the primary.

scenes.head: Sharding by user id
scenes.say: The primary can't keep up? You shard. Split rows across databases by a key. Here the key is user id, and the rule is user id modulo four, the remainder after dividing by four. Seven goes to database three. Twelve goes to zero. Why user id? Millions of values, spread evenly.

output.text:
7 goes to db 3
12 goes to db 0
1001 goes to db 1

scenes.say: Your turn. Four shards become five, so the rule becomes user id modulo five. What share of users stay put? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 4 shards to 5, with user_id % N. Share that stay?

scenes.head: Adding one shard
scenes.say: About twenty percent. The chart counts users that keep their shard. The other eighty percent move. Consistent hashing, a later topic, moves fewer.

scenes.head: Why four in twenty
scenes.say: Why twenty? Take ids zero to nineteen. Only ids zero to three have the same remainder under four and five. That's four of twenty. The other sixteen move.

scenes.head: Cheap wins before new servers
scenes.say: Sharding hurts, so most teams try cheap wins first. Cache first: a page asked a thousand times? Serve it from memory. An index is a lookup shortcut, like the one at the back of a book. A queue holds slow work, like sending email, so the request returns now. A C D N serves your images from a server near the user.
rows: finds rows without scanning them all
slow work done later by a worker
images served from near the user

scenes.head: Order of attack
scenes.say: So, the order of attack. First, measure, to find the real bottleneck. Then the cheap wins. Next, scale out the stateless app tier. Then read replicas. Shard last, because once data is split, it stays split.

scenes.head: Whiteboard math
scenes.say: Now the whiteboard math. A thousand requests per app server means a hundred servers. A cache in front answers nine in ten. Ten thousand reach the database. Say eight in ten are reads, one replica takes two thousand. Four replicas. The last two thousand are writes, all on the primary. Still too much? Four shards take five hundred each. Ten thousand queries, handled.

scenes.title: Mongo or Postgres?
scenes.statement: Pick a database for orders, and another for billions of event logs. Defend both picks.

example.output: a pick and a reason each

scenes.say: Classic trap: say Mongo because it scales, and the follow-up sinks you. You have orders, and billions of event logs. Pick a store for each, with a reason. Start from the access pattern: how you'll read the data.

scenes.head: Two ways to store an order
scenes.say: Two ways to store an order. S Q L is linked spreadsheets: an orders sheet and an items sheet, joined by id. A document store keeps a folder per order, items inside. Mongo is the famous one.

items.label: Document store: a folder per order

scenes.head: Same order, two shapes
scenes.say: In S Q L, you join two tables to rebuild order seven. You get one row per item. In a document store, order seven is stored whole, items nested inside. One lookup reads it. Which product sold best across all orders? Easy in S Q L, awkward in documents.

panels.label: excerpt
panels.code:
SELECT o.id, i.sku, i.qty
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i
  ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 7;

scenes.head: How to choose
scenes.say: Shape first: if every order has the same fields, tables fit. Relationships: a join is one query, not two round trips from your code. Transactions: moving money between two rows must be all or nothing. Scaling: Postgres grows up. Key-value stores, giant dictionaries, spread across machines. Schema: someone checks every field. The database, or your code at three a.m.
rows: duplicate, or look up in code

scenes.say: Your turn. Billions of log lines a day, read back by key, never joined. Which store fits best? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Billions of log lines, read by key, never joined. Best store?

scenes.head: Match data to store
scenes.say: A key-value or wide-column store. Wide-column means one key holds many columns, like a user's day of logs. Money needs Postgres, because a payment is all or nothing. Carts and sessions are one lookup by key, so key-value again. Odd extra fields? Postgres JSONB holds them, no second database. Every pick, defended.

scenes.title: The network splits
scenes.statement: Two data centers lose contact, and a user reads from one of them. Answer with stale data, or refuse?

example.input: link down; x=2 written on A; read on B

scenes.say: Last: a backhoe cuts the cable between two data centers. A write lands on A. A read lands on B, which never heard about it. Old data, or an error? B must pick one, and so must you.

scenes.head: Two bank branches
scenes.say: Two bank branches share one account, balance one hundred. The phone line between them goes down. A customer withdraws forty at branch A. Branch B can't know. Someone asks B for the balance. Guess one hundred, or say come back later? That dilemma is the C A P theorem.

scenes.head: A partition: B must choose
scenes.say: Same thing with data. Replica A and replica B hold x, which is one. The link breaks. That's a partition, and it will happen eventually. A write arrives at A, setting x to two. A accepts it. Now a read arrives at B. Consistency means every read sees the latest write. Availability means every request gets an answer. Partition is the broken link. B can't have both.
Your turn. Mid-partition, replica B holds a post's like count. Someone loads the post. Answer stale, or refuse? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Mid-partition, B holds a post's like count. B should...

scenes.head: B has two choices
scenes.say: Answer, even if stale. A like count off by three hurts nobody. That's availability. Choice one: serve its best guess. Choice two: error until the link heals. The cost? Stale reads, or failed requests. Cassandra leans available. Zookeeper and etcd lean consistent: they hold locks and settings.

scenes.head: Eventual consistency, healed
scenes.say: Choosing availability gives you eventual consistency: replicas disagree for a while, then agree. Each value carries a timestamp. A holds two at time five. B still says one. After the link heals, merge keeps the newest. Both now say two. Fine for likes and feeds, wrong for balances.

panels.code:
def merge(p, q):
    return max(p, q, key=lambda v: v[1])
a, b = (1, 0), (1, 0)
a = (2, 5)
print("B says", b[0])
a = b = merge(a, b)
print("healed", a[0], b[0])

scenes.head: CAP myths in interviews
scenes.say: Interviewers set traps here. Pick any two of three? No. Networks split anyway. Then you choose C or A. Eventual consistency is bad? Fine for a feed, wrong for a balance. Two writes clash? Last write wins silently drops one. Version vectors keep a counter per replica, so you can see the clash and merge.
rows: Partitions happen: choose C or A during one
a counter per replica: clash spotted

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you scale a service? Measure, add a cache, then replicas, and shard last. Up or out? Out, behind a load balancer, because one box hits a ceiling. Why stateless? So any server can take any request. Replica lag? Read your own writes from the primary. Biggest mistake? Scaling before you measure.
rows: Out, behind a load balancer: no ceiling
Any server can take any request
Read your own writes from the primary

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: S Q L or No S Q L? Start with Postgres, for joins and transactions. Pick No S Q L for huge scale or simple key lookups. Odd extra fields? Postgres has JSONB. The classic mistake is picking No S Q L because it's trendy. Pick by access pattern.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Explain C A P. In a partition, choose consistency or availability: latest write, or any answer. Pick any two? No, partitions aren't optional. Eventual consistency? Replicas agree later, fine for likes. Conflicting writes? Last write wins, or version vectors to spot the clash.
rows: In a partition: C (latest write) or A (always answers)
Replicas agree later; fine for likes

scenes.head: Build these next
scenes.say: Three things to try this week. Run two app copies and watch a login vanish. Move sessions to Redis. Count how many ids move from four shards to five: about eighty percent. Explain C A P to a friend with bank branches. If they follow, you're ready.
So say this. Measure first, then cache, stateless servers, replicas, and shard last. Start with Postgres, and choose NoSQL for access patterns. In a partition, pick consistency or availability.
lines: Measure; cache, scale out, replicas; shard last.
Postgres first; NoSQL for the access pattern.
In a partition: consistent or available.
